title: "Personnel: Who's on the Field Before Anything Else"
subtitle: "Two digits, said before the huddle breaks, that tell you who the offense brought, what the defense will send back, and how the odds of a run or a pass have already moved."
description: "How to decode personnel groupings (11, 12, 21, 13, 22, 10, 20, 00 and jumbo), why personnel is the first clue of every pre-snap read, how and why the defense matches the offense's substitutions, what ten seasons of data say about personnel and run/pass, and how the league's personnel mix rose, peaked and shifted between 2016 and 2025."
glossary:
  "Personnel grouping": "The mix of running backs, tight ends and wide receivers an offense has on the field for a play, written as two digits: running backs first, tight ends second, so '12' means one back and two tight ends (and therefore two wide receivers)."
  "11 personnel": "One running back, one tight end and three wide receivers. The NFL's most common grouping, used on roughly 60% of plays in 2016-2025."
  "12 personnel": "One running back, two tight ends and two wide receivers. The NFL's second most common grouping and close to a coin flip between run and pass."
  "13 personnel": "One running back, three tight ends and one wide receiver. A heavy grouping for short yardage and the running game."
  "21 personnel": "Two running backs (usually a fullback and a tailback), one tight end and two wide receivers. The classic I-formation grouping."
  "22 personnel": "Two running backs, two tight ends and one wide receiver. One of the heaviest common groupings, used mostly to run."
  "10 personnel": "One running back, no tight end and four wide receivers. A spread grouping that is rare in the NFL and common in college."
  "Substitution matching": "The defense changing its players in answer to the offense's personnel: more defensive backs against more receivers, more linebackers and linemen against more tight ends and backs. NFL rules protect it: when the offense substitutes, the defense must get a chance to respond before the snap."
  "Heavy personnel": "Any grouping with fewer than three wide receivers, so more tight ends, backs or linemen on the field. 12, 21, 13 and 22 are the common ones; some people keep the word for the very biggest groupings (13, 22, jumbo)."
  "Jumbo (six offensive linemen)": "A grouping with a sixth offensive lineman on the field, usually standing where a tight end would. He is ineligible to catch a pass unless he reports to the referee as eligible before the play."

``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (shared helpers for this chapter's diagrams)"}
import os
import re

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib import animation
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, FancyBboxPatch, Rectangle
from IPython.display import HTML, display

from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, defense, routes as r, style, draw_marker
from gridiron.field import FIELD_WIDTH
from gridiron.formations import LINE_D, OFF_BALL, TE_W, WING_W, OL_SPLIT

style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")

RB_RING = style.THIRD          # aqua ring: a running back (tailback or fullback)
TE_RING = style.LINE_TO_GAIN   # gold ring: a tight end
OL_RING = "#4a3aa7"            # purple ring: a sixth offensive lineman
UC, GUN, PISTOL, FB_D, TB_D = -1.9, -5.0, -3.5, -4.5, -7.0   # QB and back depths (yards)


def line5():
    """The five offensive linemen; only the center is lettered."""
    return [Player(k, k, "off", LINE_D, w, label=("C" if k == "C" else ""))
            for k, w in [("LT", -2 * OL_SPLIT), ("LG", -OL_SPLIT), ("C", 0.0),
                         ("RG", OL_SPLIT), ("RT", 2 * OL_SPLIT)]]


def P(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    """One offensive skill player at (d, w): d = yards from the ball (negative = backfield),
    w = yards to the offense's right."""
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label or key)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def ring_by_body(p, skip=()):
    """Ring every back (aqua) and tight end (gold): count the rings and you have the personnel."""
    for k, pl in p.players.items():
        if k in skip or pl.side != "off":
            continue
        if pl.pos in ("RB", "FB"):
            p.highlight(k, color=RB_RING)
        elif pl.pos == "TE":
            p.highlight(k, color=TE_RING)
    return p


def body_count(players):
    off = [q for q in players if q.side == "off"]
    rb = sum(q.pos in ("RB", "FB") for q in off)
    te = sum(q.pos == "TE" for q in off)
    wr = sum(q.pos == "WR" for q in off)
    return rb, te, wr


def card_title(ax, code, players):
    rb, te, wr = body_count(players)
    ax.text(0.0, 1.03, f"{code} personnel", transform=ax.transAxes, ha="left", va="bottom",
            fontsize=10, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
    ax.text(1.0, 1.03, f"{rb} RB · {te} TE · {wr} WR", transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right",
            va="bottom", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)


def ring_legend(fig, extra=(), y=0.0, ncol=4):
    h = [Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=9, markerfacecolor=style.OFFENSE, markeredgecolor=RB_RING,
                markeredgewidth=2.2, label="running back (R, F)"),
         Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=9, markerfacecolor=style.OFFENSE, markeredgecolor=TE_RING,
                markeredgewidth=2.2, label="tight end"),
         Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", ms=9, markerfacecolor=style.OFFENSE, markeredgecolor="white",
                label="no ring: wide receiver, QB (Q), line")]
    h += list(extra)
    fig.legend(handles=h, loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, y), ncol=ncol, fontsize=7.5,
               frameon=False, handletextpad=0.3, columnspacing=1.2)


def html_video(anim):
    """Embed a matplotlib animation in the HTML build (mp4 if ffmpeg exists, else a JS player)."""
    import shutil
    if shutil.which("ffmpeg"):
        html = anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
    else:
        html = anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once")
    plt.close(anim._fig)
    display(HTML(html))


# --- The personnel "card deck": one neutral, legal alignment per grouping (strength to the right).
# Every card has seven men on the line: the five linemen plus the two players at the ends.
CARDS = {
    "11": [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W),
           P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -12.5), P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -7.5), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 12.5)],
    "12": [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W),
           P("U", "TE", LINE_D, -TE_W), P("X", "WR", OFF_BALL, -12.5), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 12.5)],
    "21": [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("FB", "FB", FB_D, 0, "F"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"),
           P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -12.5), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 12.5)],
    "13": [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"), P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W),
           P("U", "TE", LINE_D, -TE_W), P("H", "TE", -1.7, 7.3), P("X", "WR", OFF_BALL, -12.5)],
    "10": [P("QB", "QB", GUN, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.2, "R"), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -12.5),
           P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -7.5), P("Y", "WR", OFF_BALL, 7.5), P("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 12.5)],
    "20": [P("QB", "QB", GUN, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.2, "R"), P("FB", "RB", GUN, 2.2, "F"),
           P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -12.5), P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 7.5), P("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 12.5)],
    "22": [P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("FB", "FB", FB_D, 0, "F"), P("RB", "RB", TB_D, 0, "R"),
           P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W), P("U", "TE", LINE_D, -TE_W), P("Z", "WR", OFF_BALL, 12.5)],
    "00": [P("QB", "QB", GUN, 0, "Q"), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -13.0), P("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -8.0),
           P("Y", "WR", OFF_BALL, 5.8), P("F", "WR", OFF_BALL, 9.5), P("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 13.2)],
}


def hide_yard_numbers(ax):
    """Drop the faint painted field numbers (they sit where the receivers stand in these zoomed cards)."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() is not None and abs(t.get_alpha() - 0.55) < 1e-6:
            t.remove()


def card_deck(codes):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.0))
    for ax, code in zip(axes.flat, codes):
        players = line5() + CARDS[code]
        p = ring_by_body(Play(players, None, los=35, to_go=None))
        p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-15.5, 15.5), window=(-9.5, 2.6), title=False)
        hide_yard_numbers(ax)
        card_title(ax, code, players)
    fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.93, bottom=0.11, hspace=0.42, wspace=0.05)
    ring_legend(fig, ncol=3)
    return fig
```
:::


Third-and-1 at midfield, early in the fourth quarter. The previous play has barely been whistled
dead when the broadcast cuts wide: two wide receivers jog toward their own sideline, and two
bigger men, a tight end and a fullback, run the other way to join the huddle. Across the field,
the defense reacts within a couple of seconds. A cornerback sprints off, a 245-pound linebacker
sprints on, and someone near the defensive bench is shouting a single word. The ball hasn't been
snapped, the offense hasn't even lined up, and the analyst says "they've gone to 22 personnel."
He's right, and both teams have already made a move. This chapter is about that move: who the
offense chooses to put on the field, how the defense answers (and why it swapped only one player
when the offense swapped two), who that shouting man is, and how much those two digits tell you
about what's coming.

**You'll be able to…**

- Decode any two-digit personnel label (11, 12, 21, 13, 22, 10, 20, 00) into running backs,
  tight ends and wide receivers, and recognize jumbo (a sixth lineman).
- Count the personnel yourself between plays, by watching who runs on and off.
- Explain why personnel is the first pre-snap clue and how it forces the defense's substitutions.
- Explain the substitution rules that give the defense the right to match, and how offenses use
  or deny that right.
- Read the league's personnel trends from 2016 to 2025, including the 2025 shift toward bigger
  groupings.
- Turn personnel into a first run/pass guess with real numbers, and say why it is only a first
  guess.

## Eleven players, but only five that change

Start with a puzzle. An offense has eleven players on the field, and the label for who they are
has only two digits. How can two digits describe eleven people?

Because six of the eleven almost never change. Every normal offensive snap has a
[quarterback](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd) and five
[offensive linemen](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd) (the center, two guards and two
tackles, the big men who block and, by rule, can't catch a forward pass). Those six are the
fixed core. The other five spots are the variables, and they can be filled by three kinds of
player that [The Twenty-Two](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd) introduced as the
[skill positions](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd):

- **Running backs.** Players who line up behind the line, mostly to carry the ball or block. The
  **tailback** (or halfback) is the runner; the **fullback** is a bigger back who mostly blocks
  for him. Both count as running backs here.
- **Tight ends.** Big, versatile players, usually 245 to 265 pounds, who often line up right
  next to a tackle. They block like small linemen *and* catch passes.
- **Wide receivers.** Usually the lightest and fastest on the offense, lined up wide, mainly to
  catch passes.

Every way of filling those five spots is a [**personnel
grouping**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-personnel-grouping): the mix of running backs, tight
ends and wide receivers on the field for a play. Coaches, scouts, broadcasters and the data all
write it the same way, as two digits:

> **First digit = running backs. Second digit = tight ends. Wide receivers = 5 − backs − tight ends.**

So "one-one," usually just said "eleven," means one back and one tight end, which leaves three
wide receivers. "Twelve" (one-two) is one back and two tight ends, so two receivers. "Twenty-one"
is two backs, one tight end and two receivers. You never need a third digit, because the
receivers are whatever is left over. (One grouping, jumbo, bends the arithmetic; it gets its own
section below.)

The digits are the shared language of scouting reports, broadcasts and data. Inside a team's own
playbook, groupings often carry word names instead, and the words differ from team to team (one
Houston Texans explainer mentions "Pony" and "Rabbit" for kinds of two-back grouping).[^words] When
you hear an unfamiliar word on a sideline microphone, it is probably a team's private name for
one of the groupings below.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**The digits are not jersey numbers, and "11 personnel" does not mean "the eleven players."** It
is a count of body types: one running back, one tight end. Say it "eleven" or "one-one," but
read it as two separate digits. Defensive labels count differently: a "4-2-5" means four linemen,
two linebackers and five defensive backs. Older names such as "4-3" leave off the defensive
backs because four was taken for granted. [A First Look at
Defense](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) owns those names.
:::

Why count only backs and tight ends? Because those are the two body types that change what the
offense can do *and* what the defense must fear. A tight end is a blocker who can run routes; a
fullback is a blocker who can carry the ball or catch it out of the backfield. Each one you add
makes the offense bigger and better at running the ball, and takes away a wide receiver, the
player most dangerous in the open field. The two digits are, in effect, a dial between "big" and
"fast."

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In *Madden* you pick a formation and the right players appear in it, and the computer's defense
swaps its own players instantly. In the NFL, personnel is a separate decision made **before** the
formation and the play. A coach shouts or signals the grouping ("Twelve! Twelve!"), the players
in that package run on, and the defense has to *see* them, decide, and send its own substitutes.
It takes several seconds of the [forty-second play
clock](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd), in plain view: the first thing you
can read.
:::

## Reading the deck: the eight groupings you'll meet

Here are the eight groupings the chapter asks you to know, each drawn in an ordinary, legal
alignment. Don't worry yet about the names of the alignments. Those are
[formations](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd), the next chapter's job. For now, count
the rings: an aqua ring is a running back, a gold ring is a tight end, and anyone with no ring
(apart from the quarterback and the linemen) is a wide receiver.

::: {#cell-fig-deck-everyday .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
card_deck(["11", "12", "21", "13"])
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![The four everyday groupings. Count the rings: aqua = running backs (R is the tailback, F the fullback), gold = tight ends; unringed players outside the line are wide receivers (X, Z, H). In 13 personnel the third tight end stands just outside and behind the right tight end (a 'wing') and wears the letter H: the letters name spots in the formation, not body types, which is why the ring, not the letter, tells you what he is. Seven men are on the line in every card: the five linemen (only the center, C, is lettered) plus the two players at the ends.](02-01-personnel-groupings_files/figure-html/fig-deck-everyday-output-1.svg){#fig-deck-everyday}
:::
:::


The letters on the receivers are the names most playbooks use for their *spots*: **X** is the
receiver usually on the line on one side (the "split end"), **Z** the receiver off the line on
the other side (the "flanker"), **Y** usually the tight end, and **H** or **F** a player the
offense moves around, who can be a slot receiver, a second tight end or a fullback depending on
the grouping. Look at the 12 card and you'll see X standing *off* the line: with a tight end on
the line at each end, both receivers have to step back so the tight ends stay the end men, and
eligible. [Formation Rules and the Language of
Alignment](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) explains the letters and that rule
properly. In this chapter they're just name tags; the rings do the counting.

[**11 personnel**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-11-personnel) **(1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR)** is the
NFL's default: it was on the field for about six plays in ten every season from 2016 to
2025. Its appeal is that it can do almost anything. Three wide receivers stretch the defense
across the field; the one tight end can stay in to block or run a route; the one back can run,
block a blitzer or catch. Because the offense can run or pass from it with almost equal ease,
it gives the defense very little to go on. It also forces the defense to answer with a fifth
defensive back, which we'll see is the whole substitution game in miniature.

[**12 personnel**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-12-personnel) **(1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR)** swaps the
third receiver for a second tight end. Now the offense can line up with a blocker next
to *both* tackles and run either way, or split one of the tight ends out like a receiver and
throw. It is the league's second most common grouping and, as the data below shows, the closest
thing football has to a coin flip.

[**21 personnel**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-21-personnel) **(2 RB, 1 TE, 2 WR)** adds a
fullback, the old-fashioned lead blocker. This is the grouping of the classic
I-formation (fullback directly in front of the tailback) and of the old
[pro set](02-03-classic-formations.qmd) (two backs side by side behind the quarterback), the
standard NFL look of an earlier era. A good fullback
gives the offense an extra blocker who starts moving before the defense knows where the play is
going.

[**13 personnel**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-13-personnel) **(1 RB, 3 TE, 1 WR)** is three
tight ends and just one receiver. It is mostly a short-yardage and running grouping,
though as you'll see in the film room, one team in 2025 turned it into a weapon for both.

::: {#cell-fig-deck-edges .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
card_deck(["10", "20", "22", "00"])
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Four groupings at the edges. 10 and 00 personnel are spread groupings, so the quarterback is in the shotgun (about five yards behind the center) and wide receivers fill the Y and F spots that a tight end or back would fill in other groupings. 20 personnel puts two backs beside the quarterback. 22 personnel is the old power look: fullback, tailback and a tight end on each side, with one receiver.](02-01-personnel-groupings_files/figure-html/fig-deck-edges-output-1.svg){#fig-deck-edges}
:::
:::


[**22 personnel**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-22-personnel) **(2 RB, 2 TE, 1 WR)** is the
heavy end of the everyday menu: a fullback, a tailback and two tight ends, leaving one
receiver. The offense is telling the defense, more or less, "we're going to run, and we're
bringing extra people to block for it." That's useful near the goal line, on third-and-1, and
late in a game when the offense wants to keep the clock running. It is also, for exactly that
reason, a great place to fake a run and throw (more on that trade below).

[**10 personnel**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-10-personnel) **(1 RB, 0 TE, 4 WR)** drops the
tight end for a fourth receiver. It's everywhere in college football, where spread
offenses grew up, but rare in the NFL (around 1% of plays in recent seasons). NFL offenses want
a tight end's blocking against much bigger pass rushers, and four receivers are easy for a
defense to answer: it just sends in a sixth defensive back. A good tight end is harder to match,
because no substitute is both big enough to take on his block and fast enough to cover him.

**20 personnel (2 RB, 0 TE, 3 WR)** puts two backs next to the quarterback in the shotgun with
three receivers. It's a niche look (about 1% of NFL plays or less), but a handy one: either back can
take a handoff, block, or slip out for a pass. **00 personnel** is five wide receivers and no
back at all, an "empty" backfield with nobody beside the quarterback. In the NFL it's so rare that
you may not see it all season.[^share] (Empty *formations*, in which the back or tight end lines up
wide, are common. That's a formation, not a personnel grouping, and it's the subject of
[Spread Formations](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd).)

There are a handful of other combinations, such as 01, 02, 23 and the occasional 30, but together
they make up only a percent or two of plays. If you can read the eight above, you can read
practically every NFL snap.

### Personnel is who, not where

One more rule before we move on, and it's the one beginners trip over. **Personnel counts who the
players are, not where they stand.** A tight end who lines up out wide like a receiver is still a
tight end, so the grouping is still 12 if there are two of them. A running back who lines up in
the slot is still a running back. A wide receiver standing in the backfield is still a receiver.

That's not pedantry; it's why personnel matters. The defense chooses its players by who comes on
the field, and only *then* does the offense line up. Send in two tight ends, get bigger defenders;
then spread those tight ends out like receivers, and bigger, slower players have to cover them.
That gap between personnel and formation is one of the oldest tricks in football, and you can't
see it unless you count first.

The hard case is a player whose *body* doesn't match his *label*. Deebo Samuel was a 49ers wide
receiver who, in 2021, also carried the ball 59 times for 365 yards and eight touchdowns.[^hybrid]
With him in the backfield, a grouping that reads "11" on paper played like two backs. The
Saints have used Taysom Hill, a quarterback, as a runner, a receiver and a tight end; the data
lists him as a quarterback in 2023 and 2025 and as a tight end in 2024, so the same kind of
snap gets a different label in different seasons. The Ravens' Patrick Ricard has played both
defensive line and fullback. Offenses use players like these on purpose: the defense
picks its substitutes by *label*, and a player who is two things at once makes every answer
partly wrong. Note it in your log whenever you see one.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"You can tell the position by the jersey number."** Not reliably, not any more. Before 2021,
NFL tight ends wore numbers in the 80s (or 40s), and receivers wore 80s or 10–19. Since the
league loosened its numbering rules in 2021 and again in 2023, tight ends, receivers and backs
can all wear single digits and most of the same ranges[^jersey]
([The Twenty-Two](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd) has the details). On TV, use three
other clues. **Size:** tight ends are usually 245 to 265 pounds, receivers well under that.
**Stance:** a tight end next to the tackle usually sets in a
[three-point stance](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd), one hand down like a
lineman, while receivers stand up. **Homework:** a glance at the team's roster before kickoff,
plus the analyst, who will often name the grouping for you.
:::

### Heavy personnel

You'll hear broadcasters say an offense "went heavy." [**Heavy
personnel**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-heavy-personnel) means any grouping with fewer than
three wide receivers: the offense has taken receivers off and put tight ends, backs or linemen
on. So 12, 21, 13 and 22 are all heavy (some people keep the word for 13, 22 and jumbo; this
course uses the wider meaning, as NFL Next Gen Stats does). Why take a fast player off the field?
**To block more people**, since each tight end or fullback is an extra blocker who can also be a
threat; **to make the defense get bigger**, and so slower in coverage; and **to hide the play**,
because a defense facing players who can run *and* catch can't relax against either.

## Jumbo: when a sixth lineman comes in

Sometimes even three tight ends isn't big enough. In a [**jumbo**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-jumbo-six-offensive-linemen)
grouping, the offense puts a **sixth offensive lineman** on the field, usually lined up exactly
where a tight end would be, at the end of the line next to a tackle. (Some teams put him
*inside* instead, with two tackles side by side on one end of the line; that
[unbalanced line](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd) is a formation trick for a later
chapter.) He's a lineman, often 300 pounds or more, so he blocks much better than any tight end.
That's the point: on the goal line, on third-and-1, or when killing the clock with a lead, the
offense wants raw size.

Jumbo is where the two-digit arithmetic needs one adjustment. The sixth lineman takes one of the
five changeable spots, so only **four** are left for backs, tight ends and receivers:
**receivers = 4 − backs − tight ends.** The jumbo below has one back and two tight ends, so one
receiver, not two.

::: {#cell-fig-jumbo .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = line5() + [
    Player("E6", "OL", "off", LINE_D, -TE_W, label="79"),
    P("QB", "QB", UC, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", -6.5, 0, "R"),
    P("Y", "TE", LINE_D, TE_W), P("U", "TE", -1.6, 7.2),      # a legal wing, clear of Y's ring
    P("X", "WR", OFF_BALL, -11.0),
]
```

There is a catch, and it is a rule, not a strategy. Linemen wear numbers in the 50–79 range, and a
player wearing one of those numbers is **ineligible** to catch a forward pass (he can block, but
not go out for a ball thrown past the line) unless he **reports** to the referee before the snap.
The referee then announces it, often over the stadium microphone ("Number 79 is reporting as
eligible"), so the defense knows. The full rules for eligibility and reporting are in [Formation
Rules](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd), which owns them; for now it's enough to know
that a jumbo lineman is a blocker by default and a receiver only by announcement.

So is the picture above "12" or "13"? It depends who's counting. The data used in this chapter
labels players by roster position, so it calls this snap "12" (one back, two tight ends) plus an
extra lineman, and by the jumbo rule that leaves one receiver. Some charters and staffs count a
lineman standing at tight end *as* a tight end and call it "13"; others write "12 jumbo" or
"6 OL." In the charts below, jumbo plays keep the code their backs and tight ends give them, and
are also counted separately as **jumbo**.

Jumbo is the most predictable grouping in football. In neutral situations from 2023 to 2025,
offenses in jumbo threw on fewer than one play in three. That predictability is the cost: when the
defense *knows* a run is coming, it can load up for it. It is also the opportunity, as the Detroit
Lions showed, because a defense that is sure of the run is the easiest one to fool with a pass.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Detroit Lions 2022–2024"}
Under offensive coordinator Ben Johnson (2022–2024), the Lions made the eligible lineman a regular
part of their offense. Backup tackle Dan Skipper was the usual extra lineman, and he or, on the odd
trick play, starting left tackle Taylor Decker could report eligible. In 2022 Detroit used a sixth
lineman on about 10% of its snaps, second-most in the league.

The most famous of those snaps didn't count. On December 30, 2023, at Dallas, Detroit scored a
touchdown with 23 seconds left to pull within a point at 20–19 and went for two. Jared Goff threw to Decker, who
caught it in the end zone. The officials ruled that it was Skipper, not Decker, who had reported
eligible, so Decker was an ineligible receiver. The conversion was wiped out and Detroit had to
try again from farther back: the next attempt was intercepted but erased by a Dallas offside
penalty, the one after that fell incomplete, and the Cowboys won 20–19.[^lionstwo] The play became a national argument about reporting, and it shows the logic of
jumbo: the defense saw six linemen and expected a run; the Lions' answer was a pass to a lineman.

**What to notice:** when an offense goes jumbo, watch the referee. If he turns to the press box and
announces a number, a lineman has reported eligible, and the defense now has to account for him
too.
:::

## The defense answers: substitution matching

Personnel is a two-sided game. The offense picks its eleven first, and the defense answers with its
own. Defensive groupings are named differently, usually by how many **defensive backs**
([cornerbacks](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd) and
[safeties](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd), the players whose main job is pass
coverage) are on the field, because that number is what the defense changes most:

- **Base**: four defensive backs, with seven players up front (four linemen and three
  linebackers in a "4-3," or three and four in a "3-4"). Built to stop the run.
- **Nickel**: five defensive backs. The fifth, called the **nickel back** or
  [slot cornerback](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd), usually replaces a linebacker and
  covers the receiver lined up in the slot (between the outside receiver and the line).
- **Dime**: six defensive backs, for obvious passing downs.

[A First Look at Defense](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) builds these packages properly.

The defense's choice follows a simple logic: **match bodies to bodies.** A wide receiver is fast,
so he should be covered by a defensive back, who is also fast. A tight end or fullback is big, so a
linebacker, who is bigger and better at taking on blocks, is a reasonable match. More receivers,
more defensive backs; more tight ends and backs, more linebackers. That reflex is called
[**substitution matching**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-substitution-matching).

It is a direction, not a one-for-one swap, because the defense has a **floor of four defensive
backs**: two cornerbacks and two safeties. Even 22 personnel sends five eligible receivers out
on every play, and any of them can run deep, so a defense without two corners and two safeties
has nobody left to stop the long pass. Only where there is no room for a long pass, near the
goal line or on the shortest yardage, does a defense go below four. That is why the opening
play worked the way it did: the offense swapped two receivers for two big men (11 to 22), but the
defense, already at five defensive backs, could only come down one, to four. Against 22 in 2025,
defenses kept exactly four defensive backs on about three snaps in four, and went to three or
fewer only about one in seven, mostly at the goal line or on third- and fourth-and-short.[^floor]

**Who makes the call?** The "single word" from the defensive bench is the name of the package:
"Base!" or "Nickel!", or a team's own code word for it. Someone on every defensive staff is
watching for the offense's substitutes the moment the whistle blows and calls out the grouping;
the defensive play-caller answers with the package, the substitutes run on, and the
[green dot](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd) and sideline signals do the
rest. Coordinators talk about wanting to see the offense's personnel "as early as possible," and
players notice when that relay is slow.[^caller] It is also why the hybrid players above are
worth so much to an offense: the caller has to name the grouping in a second or two, and a
player who is both a receiver and a back has no right name.

Defenses also substitute **by situation**, not just by personnel. Most have a third-and-long
package (often dime, with a sixth defensive back and extra pass rushers) and a short-yardage or
goal-line package (more linemen, fewer defensive backs) that come on at the whistle whatever the
offense sends. The offense's personnel then decides only the fine-tuning.

``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (simulated tracking for the substitution sequence)"}
# Two groups swap players between plays. gridiron's Play schedules all pre-snap movement to finish at
# the snap, so this sequence is built as BDB-style tracking frames directly (x, y in yards, 10 frames
# per second) and drawn with gridiron's Field and draw_marker (markers a little larger than usual,
# because the whole width of the field has to fit in each small panel).
LOS, BALL_Y = 50.0, FIELD_WIDTH / 2
OFF_BENCH, DEF_BENCH = 25.6, -25.6       # the two benches are on opposite sidelines
HUDDLE_C, HUDDLE_R = (-9.5, 0.0), 2.6

# Offense in 11 personnel (singleback 2x2), then 12 personnel (two tight ends) after the swap.
ALIGN_11 = {"LT": (LINE_D, -3.2), "LG": (LINE_D, -1.6), "C": (LINE_D, 0), "RG": (LINE_D, 1.6),
            "RT": (LINE_D, 3.2), "QB": (UC, 0), "RB": (TB_D, 0), "Y": (LINE_D, TE_W),
            "X": (LINE_D, -15), "H": (OFF_BALL, -9), "Z": (OFF_BALL, 15)}
ALIGN_12 = dict(ALIGN_11, U=(LINE_D, -TE_W), X=(OFF_BALL, -15))
ALIGN_12.pop("H")
OFF_LABEL = {"C": "C", "QB": "Q", "RB": "R", "Y": "Y", "U": "U", "X": "X", "H": "H", "Z": "Z"}
OFF_POS = {"RB": "RB", "Y": "TE", "U": "TE", "X": "WR", "H": "WR", "Z": "WR", "QB": "QB"}

# The defense's nickel (4-2-5) against 11, and its base 4-3 against 12.
NICKEL = {"WDE": (1.0, -4.0), "WDT": (1.0, -0.7), "SDT": (1.0, 2.35), "SDE": (1.0, 5.4),
          "MIKE": (4.5, -1.6), "WILL": (4.5, 2.4), "NB": (5.0, -9.0),
          "LCB": (7.0, -15), "RCB": (7.0, 15), "FS": (12.0, -8.5), "SS": (12.0, 8.5)}
# Base keeps the same four linemen. The new linebacker (S) goes where the nickel back was, onto U,
# the tight end who just came in, so the front sets its strength to the left; M and W stay put.
BASE = {"WDE": (1.0, -4.0), "WDT": (1.0, -0.7), "SDT": (1.0, 2.35), "SDE": (1.0, 5.4),
        "WILL": (4.5, 2.6), "MIKE": (4.5, -1.2), "SAM": (4.0, -6.6),
        "LCB": (7.0, -15), "RCB": (7.0, 15), "FS": (12.5, 1.0), "SS": (8.0, -9.5)}
DEF_LABEL = {"WDE": "E", "SDE": "E", "WDT": "T", "SDT": "T", "WILL": "W", "MIKE": "M", "SAM": "S",
             "NB": "$", "LCB": "C", "RCB": "C", "FS": "FS", "SS": "SS"}

# Huddle: ten players in a ring, the quarterback in the middle facing them.
ring_keys = ["LT", "LG", "H", "C", "RG", "RT", "Y", "Z", "RB", "X"]   # H's spot faces his bench
HUDDLE = {k: (HUDDLE_C[0] + HUDDLE_R * np.cos(a), HUDDLE_C[1] + HUDDLE_R * np.sin(a))
          for k, a in zip(ring_keys, np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 10, endpoint=False) + np.pi / 10)}
HUDDLE["QB"] = HUDDLE_C

# Keyframes: player -> [(t, d, w), ...], t = seconds since the whistle (play clock = 40 - t).
KF = {}
for k in ALIGN_11:                                        # everyone but H: huddle, then break to 12 spots
    if k == "H":
        continue
    KF[k] = [(0, *HUDDLE[k]), (15.5, *HUDDLE[k]), (21.5, *ALIGN_12[k])]
KF["H"] = [(0, *HUDDLE["H"]), (3.0, *HUDDLE["H"]), (8.0, -9.0, OFF_BENCH), (24, -9.0, OFF_BENCH)]
KF["U"] = [(0, -11.5, OFF_BENCH), (3.0, -11.5, OFF_BENCH), (8.2, *HUDDLE["H"]),
           (15.5, *HUDDLE["H"]), (21.5, *ALIGN_12["U"])]
for k, spot in NICKEL.items():                            # defense waits in nickel, then adjusts to 12
    if k == "NB":
        KF[k] = [(0, *spot), (9.0, *spot), (14.0, 3.0, DEF_BENCH), (24, 3.0, DEF_BENCH)]
    else:
        KF[k] = [(0, *spot), (16.0, *spot), (21.5, *BASE[k])]
KF["SAM"] = [(0, 6.0, DEF_BENCH), (9.5, 6.0, DEF_BENCH), (14.5, 4.5, -8.5), (16.0, 4.5, -8.5),
             (21.5, *BASE["SAM"])]
# The umpire stands over the ball while the offense substitutes, then steps back to his spot in the
# offensive backfield (NFL umpires have lined up behind the offense since 2010, except late in halves).
UMP = [(0, -12.5, -5.5), (3.5, -12.5, -5.5), (5.0, -0.6, 0.0), (15.0, -0.6, 0.0), (17.0, -12.0, -5.5)]


def at(kf, t):
    ts = np.array([q[0] for q in kf])
    return (float(np.interp(t, ts, [q[1] for q in kf])), float(np.interp(t, ts, [q[2] for q in kf])))


def sub_tracking(t_end=24.0, dt=0.1):
    """BDB-style tracking frames for the substitution sequence."""
    rows = []
    times = np.round(np.arange(0, t_end + 1e-9, dt), 2)
    for fid, t in enumerate(times, 1):
        for k, kf in KF.items():
            d, w = at(kf, t)
            side = "def" if k in DEF_LABEL else "off"
            lab = DEF_LABEL.get(k) if side == "def" else OFF_LABEL.get(k, "")
            rows.append(dict(frameId=fid, time=float(t), displayName=k, x=LOS + d, y=BALL_Y - w,
                             side=side, label=lab))
        rows.append(dict(frameId=fid, time=float(t), displayName="football", x=LOS, y=BALL_Y,
                         side="ball", label=""))
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"]
    return df


SUBS = {"H": style.MUTED, "U": TE_RING, "NB": style.MUTED, "SAM": style.DEFENSE}
SUB_NOTES = ["Whistle. 11 personnel in the huddle (H too);\nU and S wait on their sidelines",
             "Offense subs: H (a receiver) jogs off,\nU (a tight end) runs on. Umpire over the ball",
             "Defense matches: the nickel back\nruns off, S (a linebacker) runs on",
             "Both set: 12 personnel against\na base 4-3 (four DBs, three LBs)"]
SUB_TIMES = [1.5, 6.0, 12.5, 23.5]


def sub_panel(ax, df, t, small=True):
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=LOS, window=(-14.5, 14.5), to_go=None,
                numbers=False, hashes=True)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["displayName"].isin(list(SUBS)) & (df["time"] <= 15.5)]
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for k, g in trails.groupby("displayName"):
        px, py = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(px, py, color=style.OFFENSE if k in OFF_LABEL else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.45,
                zorder=3)
    for _, row in cur.iterrows():
        x, y = fld.xy(row["x"], row["y"])
        draw_marker(ax, float(x), float(y), row["side"], row["label"], ppy * (1.5 if small else 1.1),
                    r=0.85 if small else 0.75)
    for k, col in SUBS.items():                    # ring the four players who change
        row = cur[cur["displayName"] == k].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(row["x"], row["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.4, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.6, zorder=7))
    ud, uw = at(UMP, t)                            # the umpire: striped disc
    x, y = fld.xy(LOS + ud, BALL_Y - uw)
    ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 0.9, fc="white", ec=style.INK, lw=0.9, hatch="||||",
                        zorder=9))
    ax.text(float(x) + 1.4, float(y), "ump", fontsize=6.0 if small else 7.5, color=style.INK,
            ha="left", va="center", zorder=9, fontweight="bold")
    for wy, txt in [(OFF_BENCH, "offense's bench"), (DEF_BENCH, "defense's bench")]:
        bx, by = fld.xy(LOS + 12.9, BALL_Y - wy)
        ax.text(float(bx), float(by), txt, fontsize=6.5 if small else 8, color=style.INK_2,
                ha="left" if wy < 0 else "right", va="center", style="italic", zorder=6)
    return fld
```

Substitution matching, between two plays (simulated, BDB-format tracking; times are typical, not fixed). In this figure the rings mark only the four players who change: gray = leaving, gold = the tight end coming on, orange = the linebacker coming on. 1: the offense huddles in 11 personnel (H is in the huddle) while the defense waits in nickel ($ = nickel back); the two substitutes, U and S, wait on their own sidelines. 2: U runs on for H; the umpire ('ump', striped) stands over the ball so the offense can't snap yet. 3: the defense answers, its nickel back off and a linebacker (S) on. 4: 12 personnel lines up against a base 4-3, with S on U, the tight end who just arrived. The defense is drawn in its alignment for clarity; until the offense breaks the huddle it really stands loose, watching its sideline. Offense: Q = quarterback, R = running back, X/Z = receivers, Y/U = tight ends. Defense: E = end, T = tackle, M/W/S = linebackers, C = cornerback, FS/SS = safeties.
:::
:::


Notice two things. First, **the order**: the offense moved first and the defense second, and the
defense had no sensible way to go first, because any guess could be answered by the next
substitute. Second, **the defense only matched bodies.** It still has no idea whether the second
tight end is there to block or to run a route, and the offense hasn't chosen its formation. The
defense has spent its answer; the offense keeps its next two moves.

### The rules that protect the match

You met the rule behind panel 2 in [What a Play Really
Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd): when the offense substitutes, the umpire
stands over the ball and the snap waits until the defense has had a reasonable chance to respond,
except in the last two minutes of each half; when the offense *doesn't* substitute, there is no
pause, and a defense that changes players anyway risks twelve men on the field.[^subs] Three
details matter for personnel:

- **Any substitution starts the clock on that protection, even a like-for-like one.** Swap a tired
  receiver for a fresh receiver and the personnel hasn't changed, but the umpire still holds the
  ball. That's why fast-tempo offenses rotate players only at stoppages: one swap and their tempo is
  gone.
- **Not substituting is a weapon.** If the defense is in base against a 12-personnel offense that
  is throwing well, the offense can stay in 12, play fast, and keep those linebackers on the
  field. [In-Game Adjustments, Tempo, and the Sideline
  Battle](../08-the-chess-match/08-04-in-game-adjustments-and-tempo.qmd) builds that game out.
- **Bluffing has a limit.** An offense can't run a player on to bait the defense into a change and
  then pull him straight back off: a substitute who comes on and talks to his teammates must stay
  for at least one play, or the team is warned and then penalized.[^onedown] The fakes come in the
  formation, not in the substitution.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
**Substitution matching exists because offenses get to choose first.** The offense commits to its
*bodies* first, in plain view, and in exchange keeps the last word on the *formation* and the
*play*. The defense gets the last word on bodies, and the rules guarantee it time to use it. So the
offense picks personnel hoping the defense's best answer to *who* is the wrong answer to *where*
and *what*.
:::

### What defenses actually do

Here is how NFL defenses answered each grouping in 2025, counting the defensive backs on the field
for every regular-season run and pass:

::: {#46a17b03 .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (load ten seasons of play-by-play and participation data)"}
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

SEASONS = list(range(2016, 2026))
part = nfl().load_participation(SEASONS).to_pandas()
COLS = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "down", "play_type", "pass",
        "wp", "half_seconds_remaining", "shotgun", "ydstogo"]
plays = pbp(SEASONS, columns=COLS)
plays = plays[(plays.season_type == "REG") & plays.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"]) & plays.down.notna()]
df = plays.merge(part, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"])


def count(s, positions):
    """Sum the counts for some positions in a personnel string. Two formats exist:
    2016-2022 (NGS) '1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR' (linemen listed only when there are six or more), and
    2023-2025 (FTN) '1 C, 2 G, 1 QB, 1 RB, 2 T, 2 TE, 2 WR' (every player by roster position)."""
    if not isinstance(s, str):
        return np.nan
    return sum(int(n) for n, pos in re.findall(r"(\d+)\s+([A-Z]+)", s) if pos in positions)


op = df["offense_personnel"]
df["rb"] = op.map(lambda s: count(s, {"RB", "FB"}))       # fullbacks count as backs
df["te"] = op.map(lambda s: count(s, {"TE"}))
df["wr"] = op.map(lambda s: count(s, {"WR"}))
df["ol"] = op.map(lambda s: count(s, {"OL", "C", "G", "T"}))
df.loc[(df.season <= 2022) & (df.ol == 0), "ol"] = 5      # the NGS strings omit a normal five
df["db"] = df["defense_personnel"].map(lambda s: count(s, {"DB", "CB", "S", "FS", "SS"}))
df = df[df.rb.notna() & df.te.notna()].copy()
df["pers"] = df.rb.astype(int).astype(str) + df.te.astype(int).astype(str)
df["jumbo"] = df.ol >= 6

# "Neutral": 1st and 2nd down, win probability 20-80%, outside the last two minutes of each half.
neutral = df[df.down.isin([1, 2]) & df.wp.between(0.2, 0.8) & (df.half_seconds_remaining > 120)]
print(f"{len(df):,} regular-season runs and passes with personnel, 2016-2025")
```

The matching is strong but not mechanical. Against 11 personnel, defenses were in nickel or dime
about 93% of the time (the slot-receiver problem from [The
Twenty-Two](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd)). Against 12 and 21, though, about a third of defenses
stayed in nickel. Those are defenses making a bet: that their nickel back is good enough against
the run to survive a second tight end, and that keeping a fifth defensive back is worth it in case
the offense throws. The 2025 league as a whole played base on about 30% of snaps, up from a low of
about 20% in 2023. The offenses got bigger, so the defenses got bigger too.[^ngs]

## Why personnel is the first clue

The pre-snap read that this course builds, play by play, runs in a fixed order: **situation →
personnel → formation → motion → the defense's box and safeties → prediction**. (The checklist is
assembled step by step through Part 2, and [Motion and Shifts as
Weapons](02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd) puts it on one card.) Personnel comes right after the
situation for a simple reason: it is the first clue you can *see*, and you can see it early.

::: {#cell-fig-clue-clock .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
clues = [("Situation (down, distance, score, clock)", 40, 0, style.MUTED),
         ("Personnel (who runs on and off)", 37, 0, style.OFFENSE),
         ("Defense's personnel answer", 33, 0, "#e87ba4"),
         ("Formation (where they line up)", 17, 0, style.OFFENSE_DARK),
         ("Motion and shifts", 7, 0, style.THIRD),
         ("Defense's box and safeties (often disguised)", 5, 0, style.DEFENSE)]
```

Personnel does three jobs at once.

**It narrows the menu.** An offense in 22 can't throw to four receivers; an offense in 11 can't
line up with a tight end beside each tackle. Every grouping rules out much of the playbook and
rules in a few favorites ([Classic Formations](02-03-classic-formations.qmd) and [Spread
Formations](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd) pair them up).

**It moves the run/pass odds,** modestly for the common groupings and a lot for the heavy ones,
as the numbers below show.

**It sets up the matchups.** This is the deepest of the three. Because the defense matches
personnel and the offense then picks the formation, every grouping is a bet about what the
defense will do with its answer. Twelve personnel shows it best:

That's the bind. If the defense answers two tight ends with nickel, it has a 195-pound defensive
back near the line of scrimmage, and the offense can aim its run at him: a 250-pound tight end
walls him off, and the back runs around the spot where a linebacker should have been. If it answers with base, it has three linebackers on the field, and the offense can
spread the tight ends out and make a linebacker cover one of them down the field. The better the
tight ends are at *both* jobs, the worse the defense's choice gets. That's why great two-way tight
ends are so valuable, and it's a big part of why 12 personnel has grown: an offense with two of
them can pick whichever mismatch the defense hands it, after the defense has made its choice.

The same logic runs the other way for the defense. A defense with a safety who can tackle like a
linebacker, or a linebacker who can cover like a safety, doesn't have to choose: it can stay in
one grouping against everything and take the matchup game away. That's the idea behind the
[big nickel](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd), a nickel whose fifth defensive back is a
bigger safety rather than a small slot corner, and behind hybrid defenders in general, the defensive mirror of a Deebo
Samuel. The 2025 Seahawks, for example, played 220-pound rookie safety Nick Emmanwori as a nickel
defender.[^emman] [A First Look at Defense](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) tells that story.

## Personnel and run/pass: what the numbers say

So how much does personnel tell you about run or pass? Here is every grouping with at least 300
plays in the three most recent seasons, counting only **neutral situations**: first and second
down, outside the last two minutes of each half, with neither team far ahead or behind (win
probability between 20% and 80%). Think of neutral as "not late, not lopsided." In those
situations, the offense's choice reflects its plan rather than the scoreboard; [Tendencies: PROE,
Personnel, Motion, and Coverage](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd)
defines it formally and builds on it.

``` {.python .cell-code}
        va="center", ha="left")

ax.set_xlabel("share of plays that were dropbacks (%)", fontsize=8)
```

Three things jump out.

**The common groupings are weak clues.** In neutral situations, offenses passed on about 56% of
plays from 11 personnel and about 49% from 12. That's a nudge, not a signal. If you predicted "pass"
every time you saw 11 and "run" every time you saw 12, you'd be right about 54% of the time on
those plays, barely better than the 53% you'd get by saying "pass" on every one of them. That's
deliberate: the groupings an offense uses most are the ones it has built to do both. A team
whose 11 personnel was 80% pass would be giving away the game. Even four receivers (10
personnel) was only about 55% pass: spreading the defense out also thins the number of defenders
near the ball, which makes running easier.

**The heavy groupings are stronger clues.** From 22 personnel, offenses passed only about 36% of
the time, and from jumbo about 30%. That is also where the rare pass is most dangerous, because the
defense has loaded up for the run: the logic of
[play-action](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) (faking a handoff before
throwing).

**Personnel predicts the formation as well as the play.** From 11 personnel, offenses lined up in
the shotgun on about 70% of plays; from 13, only about 30%. Heavy personnel usually means the
quarterback under center, close to the ball. You can use that as a check on your count: if you
counted three tight ends and the quarterback is five yards deep in the shotgun, count again, or
expect something unusual.



### How much does personnel add?

Here is a blunt test. Take every neutral play from 2023 to 2025 and make the simplest guess the
situation allows: for each down and distance (first or second down; 1–3, 4–6, 7–10 or 11+ yards
to go), say whichever of run or pass is more common there. That guesser is right about 60% of the
time. Now let it see the personnel as well. It is still right about 60% of the time. On 11 and 12,
which are more than eight snaps in ten, the more common call simply doesn't change. Let it see one
more pre-snap fact, whether the quarterback is in the shotgun, and it jumps to about 66%.

::: {#e6a18ffe .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (how much does personnel add to a down-and-distance guess?)"}
def hit_rate(d, keys):
    """Guess the more common call (run or pass) in each cell of `keys`; return the share guessed right."""
    p_pass = d.groupby(keys, observed=True)["pass"].transform("mean")
    return ((p_pass >= 0.5) == (d["pass"] == 1)).mean()


def with_dist(d):
    return d.assign(dist=pd.cut(d.ydstogo, [0, 3, 6, 10, 100], labels=["1-3", "4-6", "7-10", "11+"]))


recent = with_dist(neutral[neutral.season.isin([2023, 2024, 2025])])
every = with_dist(df[df.season.isin([2023, 2024, 2025])])
HIT = {"neutral, down & distance": hit_rate(recent, ["down", "dist"]),
       "neutral, + personnel": hit_rate(recent, ["down", "dist", "pers"]),
       "neutral, + personnel + shotgun": hit_rate(recent, ["down", "dist", "pers", "shotgun"]),
       "all downs, down & distance": hit_rate(every, ["down", "dist"]),
       "all downs, + personnel": hit_rate(every, ["down", "dist", "pers"])}
print({k: round(v, 3) for k, v in HIT.items()})
assert 0.58 < HIT["neutral, down & distance"] < 0.62 and abs(HIT["neutral, + personnel"] - 0.60) < 0.02
assert 0.64 < HIT["neutral, + personnel + shotgun"] < 0.67
assert 0.61 < HIT["all downs, down & distance"] < 0.64 and 0.66 < HIT["all downs, + personnel"] < 0.69
short = every[every.down.isin([3, 4]) & (every.ydstogo <= 1)]
SHORT = short.groupby("pers")["pass"].mean()
assert SHORT["22"] < 0.2 and 0.28 < SHORT["11"] < 0.36
```
:::


So on ordinary first and second downs, personnel barely changes a simple run/pass guess. Its
worth is elsewhere: it tells you which formations are coming (and so where the quarterback will
stand), it sets up the matchups in the dilemma above, and in the situations where heavy
groupings appear, it means a lot. Count every down, not just neutral ones, and adding personnel
lifts the same guesser from about 63% to about 67%. The opening play's situation is the clearest
case: on third- or fourth-and-1 from 2023 to 2025, offenses in 22 personnel threw only about 15%
of the time, against about 32% from 11.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"Heavy personnel means run."** Only the heaviest groupings lean hard. Two tight ends threw on
about half of neutral plays, because players who can block *and* catch hide the offense's
intentions, which is exactly why offenses have moved toward them. The formation, the motion and
the defense's answer tell you more, and the next five chapters add those clues one at a time.
:::

## Personnel by season: the rise of 11, and the 2025 turn

Three wide receivers weren't always normal. Football Outsiders, charting games by hand, counted 11
personnel on about 40% of NFL plays in 2011, 46% in 2012 and 51% in 2013.[^fo] That climb, driven
by more passing, by college spread offenses supplying receivers and quarterbacks raised on
three-receiver sets, and by defenses answering with more defensive backs, finished just before
the data in this chapter begins. Different charters count slightly differently, so those numbers
don't belong on the same axis as the ones below, but the direction is clear. Here's how the mix
moved from 2016 to 2025.

For most of the decade the story is stability: 11 personnel on about 60% of plays, 12 on about
20%, 21 on about 8%, everything else sharing the rest. By the late 2010s, three receivers was
simply what an offense looked like, and Sean McVay's Rams were the extreme case of that habit.

Then 2025 moved. Eleven personnel fell to 58.8%, its lowest share of the decade, and 12 rose to
24.4%, its highest. Thirteen personnel jumped from 3.7% to 5.1%. Next Gen Stats, measuring it its
own way, found offenses with fewer than three wide receivers on 41.7% of 2025 plays, the first season
at or above 38% since it began tracking in 2016, and the share kept climbing as the season went on.[^ngs2]

Why then? No rule change or single coach set it off, and nobody can prove a cause from a
chart. The explanation most analysts give is an arms race. Through the late 2010s and early
2020s, defenses got smaller and faster to stop the pass: more nickel and dime, and more looks
with two safeties deep (which [A First Look at Defense](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)
introduces as two-high). A defense like that has fewer big bodies near the line, a
"light box," and it was winning: getting to quarterbacks faster and covering better. Offenses
answered by getting bigger, to force defenses into base, where "they generally do not want an
undersized extra DB to get steamrolled by a tight end," as an NFL.com Next Gen Stats analysis put it, and then
running at whatever was left, often with the quarterback back under center.[^why] And as you saw
above, defenses answered *that* by playing more base in 2025. Each side's move invites the
other's. [The Modern
Era](../11-history/11-05-the-modern-era.qmd) tells the whole arms race, and [Working with nflverse
Data in Python](../13-analytics-and-data/13-01-nflverse-in-python.qmd) shows you how to rebuild
these charts yourself.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: where the numbers come from"}
Every chart in this chapter is a course calculation from the nflverse **participation** data
(`load_participation()`), which lists the personnel on each play, joined to nflverse
play-by-play.[^data] Three cautions if you reproduce them. First, the source changes between 2022
and 2023: Next Gen Stats supplied 2016–2022 and FTN Data supplies 2023 onward, and the personnel
strings change format ("1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR" before, every player by position after), so the code
normalizes them before counting; the personnel shares agree across the break. Second, players
are counted by **roster position**, not by role. A snap with a second quarterback or a
defensive player in the offense (a string like "2 QB, 1 RB, 1 TE, 2 WR") is labeled by its backs
and tight ends, here "11," even though only two receivers are out there. That is about 1% of
plays, too few to move the charts, and the course keeps the simple backs-then-tight-ends count so
its numbers match the course fact sheet. Third, the participation file for a season arrives only
after the season ends, so 2026 numbers won't exist until early 2027. Published series from other providers
(Next Gen Stats, Sharp Football, PFF) count slightly differently; never put two providers' numbers on
one axis.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Los Angeles Rams 2017–2019"}
When the Rams hired Sean McVay in January 2017, he was 30, the youngest head coach in modern NFL
history.[^mcvay] His offense became famous for using one grouping, 11 personnel, almost all the time:
about 81% of plays in 2017, 93% in 2018 and 73% in 2019, against a league norm of about 60%.

Why would a coach give up the personnel game entirely? Because he was playing a different one. If
the offense never substitutes, the defense never gets a reason to, so it sits in nickel all day:
in 2018, defenses had five or more defensive backs on about 94% of the Rams' plays. That suited
McVay twice over. A nickel defense has one fewer big body near the line, so his running game
was always aimed at a lighter front. And a grouping that never changes tells the defense nothing:
in neutral situations in 2018 the Rams passed on 56% of their 11-personnel plays, almost exactly
the league rate. McVay put his variety into formation, motion and play-action instead, and it
worked: the 2018 Rams reached Super Bowl LIII.

**What to notice:** an offense that never substitutes isn't being lazy. It's denying the defense
the first clue.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: San Francisco 49ers, 21 personnel and Kyle Juszczyk"}
Kyle Shanahan's 49ers have been the league's leading 21-personnel team for most of his tenure: first
in the league in 21 personnel in 2017, 2018, 2019, 2021, 2024 and 2025, and second in the other
seasons from 2017 to 2025, typically around a third of their plays, against a league share of about
8%. The player who makes it work is fullback Kyle Juszczyk, who signed in March 2017 on a contract
that made him, at the time, the highest-paid fullback in the league.[^juice]

Juszczyk can block a linebacker on a run, line up in the slot, or split out wide like a receiver. When he lines up wide, the defense that matched
21 personnel with its base package has to send someone with him: a cornerback, which leaves a
linebacker covering a receiver somewhere else, or a linebacker, which takes a defender away from
the ball (Drill 2 below draws exactly this). Two backs also give the offense two running threats
for every play-action fake.

**What to notice:** when the 49ers come out with a fullback, find him after the huddle breaks. Where
he lines up tells you which matchup they're hunting.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Baltimore Ravens 2019"}
The 2019 Ravens, with Lamar Jackson at quarterback (that season's unanimous MVP) and Greg Roman as
offensive coordinator, set the NFL record for team rushing yards in a season, 3,296.[^ravens] They did
it big. Baltimore used 22 personnel on about 16% of its plays, more than five times the league's 3%,
with tight ends Mark Andrews, Hayden Hurst and Nick Boyle and the two-way lineman/fullback Patrick
Ricard.

The surprise is in the tendencies. In neutral situations, the Ravens *ran* on about 64% of their
11-personnel plays (the league passed 56% of the time) and *passed* on about 63% of their
12-personnel plays (league: 49%). With the most dangerous runner on the field at quarterback, three
receivers didn't mean "pass" and two tight ends didn't mean "run."

**What to notice:** league tendencies are where you start. A good scouting report, like your own
prediction log, adjusts them team by team ([The Ravens' Option Run
Game](../12-case-studies/12-05-ravens-lamar-run-game.qmd) has the full case).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2024"}
The 2024 Eagles signed Saquon Barkley, who ran for 2,005 yards, the ninth 2,000-yard season in NFL
history, and won Super Bowl LIX, 40–22 over Kansas City.[^barkley] Their personnel was the vehicle:
12 personnel on about a third of their plays (the league was at 23.5%), with tight end Dallas
Goedert and a second tight end next to the best offensive line in football.

**What to notice:** in neutral situations the Eagles passed on only 32% of their 12-personnel plays,
against 48% for the league. Everyone knew 12 meant run, and they ran anyway. Predictability costs
less when you're good enough at the thing you're predicted to do ([The Eagles: Trenches, RPOs, and
the Tush Push](../12-case-studies/12-06-eagles-trenches-and-tush-push.qmd)).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: the 2025 turn, Rams and Seahawks"}
Two NFC West teams show two different routes to the 2025 turn. McVay's Rams, the 11-personnel team
of 2018, used **13 personnel** on about 31% of their plays, far more than any other team (the next
was 13%), and 12 on only about 9%: they were a *binary* team, three receivers or three tight ends.
Matthew Stafford won the MVP.[^rams25] Defenses did match: they played base on about three of
every four Rams 13 snaps. But matching bought them little, because the big grouping didn't mean
run. In neutral situations the Rams threw on 47% of their 13-personnel plays, the league's 13
rate, almost always from under center, where a pass looks like a run until the fake. The tell was
the *light* grouping: from 11 they threw 67% of the time, against a league 57%.

The champion Seattle Seahawks, under offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak in 2025, got big the other
way: by *variety*. They used fewer than three wide receivers on about 55% of their snaps, fifth-most
in the league, spread across 11, 12, 21 and 22, with a fullback (usually Robbie Ouzts) on the
field for about 19% of their plays, on the way to beating New England 29–13 in Super Bowl LX.

**What to notice:** when the Rams show three tight ends, don't assume run; when they show three
receivers, lean pass. When Seattle subs, the fullback is the tell to watch for.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: call the personnel"}
- **Between plays, watch the sidelines, not the replay.** When the broadcast shows a wide shot, count
  who jogs off and who runs on. Two receivers off and a tight end and a fullback on is a change from
  11 to 22.
- **Count backs, then tight ends, and say the number out loud.** Backs stand behind or beside the
  quarterback; tight ends are the big players at the end of the line or just behind it, usually with
  a hand down. Receivers are what's left: 5 minus the other two (4 minus, if there's a sixth lineman).
- **Look for a sixth lineman.** A 300-pounder standing where a tight end usually stands means jumbo.
  Listen for the referee's "reporting as eligible."
- **Then watch the defense.** Did a defensive back run off or a linebacker run on? Base, nickel or
  dime? If the offense substituted and the defense *didn't*, the defense is making a bet.
- **Make your first guess from the numbers** (neutral downs, 2023–2025): 11 about 56% pass, 12 about
  49%, 13 about 45%, 22 about 36%, jumbo about 30%. Treat 11 and 12 as coin flips with a lean; treat
  22 and jumbo, especially on third-and-short, as run unless something says otherwise. Then adjust
  for down and distance, where the quarterback stands, and what you know about the team.
- **Write it down.** Add a "personnel" column to your [prediction
  log](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd): grouping, your guess, the result. After a
  half, compare your hit rate on the heavy groupings with your hit rate on 11.
:::

**What's the personnel, which defensive package should you expect, and does the grouping lean run or
pass?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**13 personnel.** The weights do the work. #87, #81 and #88 are all 250 pounds or more: tight-end
bodies, and the two with a hand down are standing where tight ends stand. #26, at 215 and behind the
quarterback, is the back. #11, at 195, is the only receiver. One back, three tight ends: 13. It
doesn't matter that #81 is standing out wide where a receiver usually lines up; he is a 250-pound
tight end wherever he stands.

**The defense:** against 13 personnel in 2025, defenses played their base package (four defensive
backs) about 80% of the time, and went to nickel only about 13%. Expect linebackers.

**Run or pass:** on neutral downs, 13 personnel leaned run, with passes on about 45% of plays. Now
look at #81. A base defense has two cornerbacks, and one of them will probably go out with him. That
corner is fine in coverage, but on a run he is a 195-pound defender being blocked by a 250-pound tight
end, and he is the man who is supposed to turn the run back inside. If the defense sends a
linebacker or safety instead, it has one fewer player near the ball. Either way the offense has
made the defense pay for its answer, the same bind as the two-tight-end dilemma. Personnel gives you
the first guess; the formation sharpens it, which is where the next chapters go.
:::
:::

Gold ring = tight end.](02-01-personnel-groupings_files/figure-html/fig-predict-fb-output-1.svg){#fig-predict-fb}

**What's the personnel? Who has the advantage now, and what is the offense hoping for?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Still 21 personnel**, even with the fullback out wide.

**Who has the advantage:** the offense. Look where the defense's players have had to go. A cornerback
went out with the fullback, so the Sam linebacker (S) has had to walk out over the slot receiver (Z):
a bigger, slower player than a nickel back, now covering a receiver. If the defense swaps those two
(corner on Z, linebacker on the fullback), it has a linebacker 15 yards from the ball instead. Either
way, a linebacker has left the area near the ball.

**What the offense is hoping for:** whichever of two good options the defense leaves. With a
linebacker on Z, a quick throw to Z. With that linebacker gone from the middle, a run: there are only
six defenders near the line (four linemen and the two remaining linebackers) against six blockers (five
linemen and the tight end), a fair fight for the tailback.

The defense has one more answer: the strong safety walks down over Z, so the Sam linebacker can stay
in the box. That keeps the Sam near the ball for the run but leaves only one safety deep, which is exactly the picture the
offense's play-action is built to beat. Every answer costs something. This is the 49ers'
21-personnel idea in one picture: the defense answered *who*, and the offense answered *where*.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: third-and-7"}
Third-and-7 at the opponent's 45. On first and second down the offense ran twice from 12 personnel (two
tight ends), and the defense matched with its base 4-3 both times. Second down ends, and fourteen
seconds later the ball is snapped from this picture:

::: {#cell-fig-predict-tempo .cell execution_count=18}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = line5() + [P("QB", "QB", GUN, 0, "Q"), P("RB", "RB", GUN, -2.2, "R"), P("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15),
                 P("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 5.6), P("U", "TE", OFF_BALL, 9.8), P("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 15)]
dfn = defense("4-3_over", "two_high", off)
fix = {"SAM": dict(d=4.5, w=7.6), "MIKE": dict(d=5.0, w=2.0), "WILL": dict(d=4.8, w=-3.4),
       "SS": dict(d=10.0, w=10.0), "FS": dict(d=13.0, w=-2.0), "LCB": dict(d=6.5), "RCB": dict(d=6.5)}
dfn = [q2.moved(**fix[q2.key]) if q2.key in fix else q2 for q2 in dfn]
q = Play(off, dfn, los=65, to_go=7)
ring_by_body(q)
q.draw(lateral=(-19, 19), window=(-7.5, 15), title=False)
hide_yard_numbers(plt.gca())
plt.show()
```

**Count both teams' personnel. What's wrong for the defense, why didn't it fix it, and what does the
offense probably want?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**What's wrong:** nothing changed. The offense is still in 12 personnel (two gold rings), and the
defense is still in base, with three linebackers, on third-and-7, a passing down. Fourteen seconds is
a no-huddle snap: the offense didn't substitute.

**Why the defense didn't fix it:** it couldn't, safely. With no offensive substitution the umpire had
no reason to stand over the ball. A defense that starts running a linebacker off and a defensive back
on while the offense is set risks twelve men on the field at the snap, five yards on third-and-7.

**What the offense wants:** a pass, probably to a tight end. The offense spent two plays teaching the
defense that this grouping runs, which kept it in base. Now both tight ends stand off the line,
split out beside Z, and linebackers have to cover them away from the ball.

If the defense saw this coming, its answer was the situational substitution from earlier in the
chapter: send its third-down package on at the whistle, *before* the offense hurried to the line,
and live with the risk of a run against a lighter defense.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Personnel is two digits: running backs, then tight ends.** Receivers fill the rest of the five
  changeable spots (5 − backs − tight ends), or four of them in jumbo, where a sixth lineman takes one.
- **Personnel counts who is on the field, not where they stand,** and the gap between personnel and
  formation is where offenses build mismatches. Hybrid players blur the count on purpose.
- **The offense commits first, and the defense matches** in direction (more receivers, more defensive
  backs; more tight ends and backs, more linebackers) down to a floor of four defensive backs. The
  rules give it time whenever the offense substitutes, and none when it doesn't.
- **Personnel shifts the odds more than it settles them.** On ordinary first and second downs it
  barely improves a down-and-distance guess; its weight shows in heavy groupings and short yardage,
  in the formation it predicts, and in the matchups it sets up.
- **The league's mix moves with the defense.** 11 personnel rose through the early 2010s, held near
  60% for a decade, then fell to a decade low in 2025 as offenses went bigger against lighter
  defenses, and defenses answered with more base.
